title: A 3,400-Year-Old Folding Chair Found in a Danish Grave
summary:
Imagine sitting on a folding chair that's over 3,000 years old. That's what happened when archaeologists dug up a burial mound in Denmark in 1891. They found a wooden folding chair that was made around 1400 B.C. That's about 3,400 years ago! It's the only completely preserved chair from the Bronze Age in Europe. The Bronze Age was a time when people used bronze, a metal made from copper and tin, for tools and weapons.

The chair was in the grave of a chieftain, a leader of a group. He was buried in a hollowed-out oak tree trunk and wrapped in a cowhide. He wore a wool cloak, two wool hats, woolen mittens, and leather shoes. His family left gifts like a bronze ax, a bronze dagger, and some wooden bowls.

The chair's frame is made of ash wood, and the seat was made of otter skin. Only a tiny piece of the skin is left. The chair was low, only about 9.5 inches off the ground. It had patterns on top, filled with a black, tar-like stuff.

Folding chairs were not just for sitting. They showed that the person was very important. Similar chairs have been found in Egypt and Greece, but this one is special because it's the only one that's whole. It shows that people in different places traded ideas. So next time you sit on a folding chair, think about the ancient chief who had one too!
why_it_matters: The next time you sit on a folding chair, think about how this simple, space-saving design has been around for thousands of years — and how everyday objects can help us understand history.

background_read: Ancient leaders were often buried with things they used in life, because people believed those items showed their importance.
The chair was found in Denmark (a country in northern Europe), where many ancient burial mounds are protected by law today.
Wood and animal skin usually rot away over thousands of years, so finding a whole wooden chair from the Bronze Age is extremely rare.
Article_Structure: WHO: A Bronze Age chieftain — a group leader — who was buried in a hollowed-out oak tree trunk around 1400 B.C.
WHAT: A 3,400-year-old wooden folding chair found in his grave, the only completely preserved chair from the Bronze Age in Europe.
WHERE: In a burial mound in Denmark, first dug up in 1891.
WHY: The chair showed status and importance; similar chairs in Egypt and Greece show that people traded ideas across regions.

perspectives.description: Unearthing a whole wooden chair from so long ago is a rare find, because most wood from that time has rotted away.
Objects like this chair tell us that ancient leaders showed power with special belongings and that distant places shared ideas.
It makes ordinary things feel exciting and shows that even a folding chair can have a fascinating story.
